LETTER TO THE EDITORS
A case of glycine-receptor antibody-associated encephalomyelitis
with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM): clinical course, treatment
and CSF ﬁndings
A. Piotrowicz • A. Thu¨men • M. I. Leite • A. Vincent •
A. Moser
Received: 8 March 2011 / Accepted: 20 April 2011 / Published online: 4 May 2011
/C211Springer-Verlag 2011
Dear Sirs,
Over several months a 58-year-old man developed muscle
stiffness, myoclonus and experienced several sudden falls
caused by sensory and acoustic stimuli. On neurological
examination, a severe startle reaction could be triggered by
unexpected noises and there was stiffness, especially of the
back and lower limb muscles, with myoclonus, lower limb
paraparesis, muscle rigidity and increased tendon reﬂexes
without further pyramidal signs. He was not able to walk
without help. He also exhibited a mild pontine syndrome
with disturbed smooth pursuit eye movements and diplo-
pia. Electrophysiological studies revealed ubiquitous early
recruitment and continuous motor unit activity as described
for stiff person syndrome by Meinck and Thompson [ 1].
Cerebral MRI scans were normal. Antibodies against glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), amphiphysin, CYFRA
21-1, CEA, Ri, Hu, Yo, MA1, MA2, CV2 and CRMP5
could not be detected in serum. Neuron-speciﬁc enolase
(NSE) enzyme concentrations were not raised. An exten-
sive cancer search including 18-F-FDG-PET, abdominal
ultrasound, X-ray of the chest and bronchoscopy was
negative. However, serum glycine receptor (GlyR) anti-
bodies were detected by a cell-based assay (Fig. 1)[ 2].
Initial lumbar puncture revealed oligoclonal IgG bands and
45 lymphocytes/ ll (normal: \4 cells/ ll) in the
cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF). GlyR antibodies could also be
found in the patient’s CSF.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glutamate
levels in CSF were measured by HPLC, with electro-
chemical detection after precolumn o-phthaldialdehyde
sulphite derivatization, in the patient’s CSF and control
samples from 10 subjects (4 males, 6 females); age range
35–83 years (mean 54 years) undergoing diagnostic lumbar
puncture as part of their investigations. Their CSF analyses
were normal and neurological disorders were excluded. All
lumbar punctures were done between 11.00 am and
2.00 pm. Their GABA levels were 42.7 ± 14.2 nmol/l. As
shown in Fig. 2, before any treatment the patient’s GABA
level was higher (89.0 nmol/l) than upper limit of the
control range (mean ? 3SDs, 85.3 nmol/l). Glutamate
levels were also lower (initial: 0.33 lmol/l; after
18 months: 0.35 lmol/l) than controls (0.49 ± 0.2 lmol/l)
although not signiﬁcantly different.
The neurological symptoms ameliorated after an initial
therapy of six plasmaphereses followed by oral cortico-
steroids (1 mg/kg body weight). The GABA
A receptor
agonist clonazepam led to a further improvement of muscle
stiffness and rigidity. Only a mild pontine symptom with
diplopia persisted. CSF GABA levels fell over the treat-
ment period to 28.5 nmol/l (18 months after initial lumbar
puncture). GlyR antibody titers also declined but were still
just detectable in the serum at 12 months (Fig. 1).
Once the improvement had stabilised for 18 months, we
tried to wean the steroids. After 2 weeks without steroids the
patient developed again neurological symptoms with a left
internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and without signs on the MRI.
Steroids were therefore increased to 0.5 mg/kg and a steroid-
sparing drug, azathioprine (2 mg/kg), was introduced. Under

this regime the patient is now without symptoms. Up to now,
medical examinations are being done every 6 months.

Neurochemical Research Group, Department of Neurology,
University of Lu¨beck, Ratzeburger Allee 160, 23538 Lu¨beck,
Germany

University of Oxford, Headley Way, Oxford OX3 9DU, UK

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a neuroimmunological,
and less often, paraneoplastic disease, with symmetrical
rigidity and muscle stiffness, particularly of axial and
proximal limb muscles, and neuropsychiatric symptoms
[3–7]. Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and
myoclonus is a rare ‘‘SPS plus’’ variant [2, 8, 9]. Meinck et al.
[5] found GAD antibodies in 80% of patients with SPS and
progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PERM), compared with 5% in patients with other neuro-
logical syndromes and 1% in normal controls. However, in a
recent report, Saiz et al. [ 10] found that 36% of 61 GAD
antibody-associated patients developed SPS while 42% had
other neurological syndromes (i.e. cerebellar ataxia, epi-
lepsy, limbic encephalitis or myasthenia gravis) but they did
not mention SPS plus or PERM. GAD antibodies may be as
an indicator for SPS or PERM disease but it is not a
requirement for the diagnosis which is based on the clinical
and electromyographic features. Although GAD antibodies
are unlikely to be directly pathogenic because they target an
intracellular antigen, they are beginning to be accepted as a
marker for an immune-mediated process that may respond
well to immunotherapies [11].
Glycine receptor antibodies were ﬁrst reported in the
serum of a patient similar to the one described here, with
negative GAD antibodies and no tumour found, by Hutch-
inson et al. [ 2]. That patient also responded well to treat-
ments, although the symptoms were serious and protracted
and the response to treatment took 2 years. In contrast to
GAD antibodies, GlyR antibodies are highly likely to be
pathogenic because they are detected by binding to the
extracellular aspects of the GlyR on intact cell lines.
Although not common, they have now been found in other
patients with PERM, SPS or hyperekplexia [12].
GABA and glycine are the most important inhibitory
neurotransmitters in the brain, brainstem, and spinal cord.
GABA
A, GABAC, and glycine receptor families represent
pentameric ligand-gated ion channels that respond to the
inhibitory neurotransmitters by opening a chloride-selec-
tive central pore lined with ﬁve transmembrane segments.
GABA as well as glycine activates chloride ion conduc-
tance, resulting in hyperpolarization of the neuronal
membrane. The inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and
glycine are of particular interest because many commonly
studied and therapeutically useful drugs work by selec-
tively affecting these two neurotransmitter systems. Espe-
cially, GABAergic drugs play an important role in reducing
muscle tone as well as inﬂuencing higher cognitive func-
tions. Thus, as described in our patient, the GABA
A
receptor agonist clonazepam ameliorated the patient’s
symptoms probably by increasing an inhibitory state of the
central nervous system.
In our PERM patient, not only GlyR antibodies were found
in serum but also increased GABA levels in the CSF. Inter-
estingly, during treatment symptoms ameliorated and in par-
allel, GlyR antibody titers declined and GABA levels
normalized. The ﬁnding of high GABA levels in our PERM
patient is in contrast to a recently published case report con-
cerning a Ri antibody-associated SPS patient with very low
GABA CSF levels; the authors s uggested a disinhibition of
excitatory neurons, perhaps due to a loss of GABAergic func-
tion with consecutive muscle hyperexcitability [ 13]. In the
GAD antibody-associated SPS form low GABA levels were

found [14], either related to loss of GABA neurons or because
GAD is the enzyme responsible for synthesis of GABA [5].
Additionally, in startle disease with GlyR gene mutations, low

CSF GABA levels were described in some sporadic cases [15],
whereas a high level was found in a familial hyperekplexia [16].
One explanation for the different GABA ﬁndings might
be that in our PERM patient, GABA levels increase to
compensate for the lack of glycine responsiveness in the
presence of antibodies that block or down-regulate gly-
cinergic neuronal inhibitory activity. Experimental studies
are required to investigate the functional effects of the
antibodies.
Conﬂict of interest None.
